title: Ballad V
text:
I give you thanks, Love
I give you
        thanks, Love,
for every grief and torment,
and from this day on I am
        content with every pain.
Content am I with all I have been able to suffer,

        Lord, in your beautiful kingdom;
for by your grace, though I deserved nothing,

        you have given me so great a gift,
since you have made me worthy
of so
        blessed a smile,

which has carried my heart to paradise.
I give you thanks,
        Love.
To paradise my heart have carried
the lovely laughing eyes,

        where I saw you, Love, hiding
with your burning flames.

        O lovely shining eyes,
that have stolen my heart!


I give you thanks, Love.
I feared for my life:
My lady
        dressed in white,
with a loving smile, came joyfully
to my aid, beautiful and
        honest:
her head was adorned
with roses and wallflowers,
and her
        eyes outshine the sun in their splendor.
I give you thanks, Love.

        Version by Carlos López Narváez
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering, identified as a version by Carlos López Narváez, rather than directly from the Italian original; the refrain, shifted lineation, and devotional address are preserved. The supplied body opens with a standalone repetition of the refrain before its next line, and that duplicate opening is retained.

title: To Death
text:
You will come all the same. Why not now?

How long I have waited. Hard times are coming.

I have put out the light and opened the door

for you, because you are magical and simple.

Take, then, whatever form pleases you most,

aim and fire a poisoned bullet at me,

or strangle me like an efficient murderer,

or infect me—the typhus would be my lot—,

or burst from the fairy tale you wrote,

the one we are tired of hearing day and night,

in which blue guards climb the stairs,

led by the caretaker, pale with fear.

It is all the same to me. The Yenisei swirls,

the North Star twinkles as it always will,

and the blue glint in my beloved's eyes

is darkened by the final horror.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering rather than directly from the Russian original; the intimate address to Death, the fairy-tale intrusion, and the final celestial imagery are retained.

title: To the City of Pushkin
text:
1


What can I do? They have destroyed you,

What a cruel encounter, this parting!

Here there was a fountain, there were alleys,

farther off the park grew green…

The dawn, rosier than dawn itself,

was that April. The smell of damp earth,

of a first kiss…


2


The leaves of this willow died in the last century,

to shine a hundred times fresher in the form of verse.

The roses changed into purple wild-rose gardens,

but the school hymns still spring forth undaunted.

Half a century passed! Divine fortune favored me,

and in violent days I forgot the flow of years.

I no longer go there! But on the bank of death's river,

I shall carry my trembling gardens of Tsarskoye Selo.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering rather than directly from the Russian original; the numbered sections, remembered landscape, and Tsarskoye Selo reference are retained.

title: Lot's Wife
text:
And the righteous man followed God's radiant messenger

up a black mountain, following in his tracks,

while a tireless voice harried the woman:

—It is not too late; you can still look back.


Toward the red towers of your native Sodom,

the courtyard where you once sang, the pavilion for spinning,

the windows of the enormous house

where your progeny sanctified your marriage bed.


One glance: a sudden stab of pain

in her eyes, before she could utter a sound.

Her body melted into transparent salt

and her light legs rooted in the earth.


Who will mourn this woman? Is she not

far too insignificant for our concern?

Even so, I shall never deny her in my heart,

she who died because she chose to turn back.




1922–24
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering rather than directly from the Russian original; the biblical scene, the speaker's sympathy for the woman, and the 1922–24 date are retained.

title: It's Sheer Nonsense That I Live in Sorrow…
text:
It's sheer nonsense that I live in sorrow

and that memory torments me.

I am no regular visitor to his lair,

yet there I feel distraught.

When I descend to the cellar with my lantern,

it seems to me once more that a muffled collapse

thunders in the narrow, steep staircase.

The lantern smokes. I cannot turn back,

and I know I am going where the enemy is.

And I will ask for mercy… but there now

everything is dark and silent. My feast is over!

Thirty years ago they escorted the lady,

thirty years since the sly old man died…

I have arrived late. What bad luck!

I can no longer show myself off anywhere,

but I brush against the paintings on the walls

and warm myself by the fireplace. How wonderful!

Through mold, ash, and blackness

two gray emeralds gleam

and the cat meows. Come, creature, let's go home!


But where is my home, and where is my sanity?
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering rather than directly from the Russian original; the descent, the abandoned feast, and the cat's emerald eyes are preserved, including the source's ellipses and final question.

title: This Cruel Age Has Led Me Astray
text:
This cruel age has led me astray

like a river driven from its course.

Diverted from familiar banks,

my changing life flowed

into a kindred channel.

How many spectacles I missed:

the curtain rising without me

and falling too. How many friends

I never had the chance to know.

Here, in the only city I can call my own,

where I could walk in my sleep without losing my way,

how many foreign skies might I have dreamed

that would not bear witness through my tears.

And how many verses I was unable to write!

Their secret choruses haunt me

very close. One day, perhaps,

they will strangle me.

I know beginnings and endings too,

and life-in-death and something else

better not remembered now.

A certain woman

has usurped my place

and uses my true name,

leaving me only a nickname

with which I have done the best I could.

The grave I go to will not be mine.

But if I could step outside myself

and look upon the person I am,

I would know, at last, what envy is.




1944
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering rather than directly from the Russian original; the river-course metaphor, theatrical absences, divided identity, and 1944 date are retained.

title: Dedication
text:
The mountains bow beneath such grief

and the gigantic river lies inert.

But the sentence has strong bolts;

behind them only prison dungeons

and a melancholy that is death.


For whom does the light breeze blow,

for whom is sunset's delight—

we do not know, the same everywhere,

we hear only the hateful screech of prison keys

and the soldier's heavy tread.


We rose as for early Mass,

we walked through the uncertain city,

to find one another, dead and lifeless,

beneath the sun or the Neva's densest fog,

but hope sings true in the distance…


The sentence… and tears suddenly spring,

already severed from everything,

as life is torn painfully from the heart,

as though she were brutally hurled backward,

but she walks… falters… alone…


Where are now those companions chance gave me,

of my years in naked hell?

In the Siberian blizzard, what do they dream,

what do they imagine in the lunar circle?

To you I send my farewell and my greeting.
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering rather than directly from the Russian original. This is one of two Spanish versions of the same Dedication; recurring images are translated consistently where the wording overlaps, while this version's prison-dungeon wording, sequence, and lack of a date are retained.

title: Dedication
text:
A pain like this could move mountains,

and reverse the course of the waters,

but it cannot spring these mighty bolts

that bar our entrance to cells

packed with those condemned to death…

For some, the fresh wind may blow,

for others sunlight fades into idleness,

but we, joined in our terror,

hear only the creak of keys

and the tread of the soldiery's heavy boots.

As though we rose for the first Mass,

day after day we crossed the desert,

walking the silent street and square,

to gather, more dead than alive.

The sun had declined, the Neva had dimmed

and hope was always singing far away.

What sentence was pronounced?… That moan,

that sudden flow of women's tears,

singles one out from the rest,

as if they had knocked her down,

tearing her heart from her breast.

Then let her go, stumbling, alone.

Where will my unnameable friends be now,

from those two years of dwelling in hell?

What specters mock them now, amid

the fury of Siberian snows,

or in the moon's clouded circle?

For them I weep, Hello and Goodbye!




1940
editorial_note: Translated from the supplied Spanish rendering rather than directly from the Russian original. This is the second Spanish version of the same Dedication as db2445ea-b57f-41b5-b89c-2853df3f9261; shared imagery is rendered consistently where possible, while this version's differing lines and 1940 date are retained.

title: One Second
text:
My hands are cold.


I have gone out into the street,

		settled the requisite banal matter,

		and returned home to take up again

		my place at this table.


		Then I discovered

		the coldness of my hands,


		a sign

		that troubles me perhaps without justification,

		because having cold hands is such a small thing.



		This cold November

		is in my hands, nothing more.


		It is me:

		I see the naively Greek vase

		and the familiar evening surrounding me.



		But for me it is very strange to have cold hands.



		In a fleeting second, my thought has seen

		the fog so likely, the gray written page

		where the name I bear would be crossed out

		with the frost ink of the end.
From "With
		the Air" (2004)
editorial_note: The translation preserves the source's staggered lineation, its ordinary errand turning into an intimation of death, and the bibliographic closing from Con el aire (2004).
